imperial.name: Swede

actions.text:
Sow

Jun for maincrop. May is possible. By early Jul use a variety that can still mature locally.

Plant out

Jun–Jul for module-raised seedlings.

methods.text:
Sow 

Make shallow drills in the final bed and sow thinly. Cover with fine soil and keep the seedbed moist. Fill a bed cleared of early salads or beans while there is still time for roots to swell.

Plant out 

Modules are an alternative if the bed is occupied. Move small seedlings before their roots fill the cells. Firm the soil and water in.

varieties.text:
Magres

A purple-topped swede with yellow flesh and good eating quality. A strong addition for an autumn and winter root crop.

Marian

A familiar purple-topped swede with pale yellow flesh.

Tweed F1

A vigorous British-bred hybrid with clubroot resistance. Useful where that disease is a concern, alongside good rotation and soil care.

Joan

Good-flavoured roots for autumn cropping. Sow in late spring or early summer.

Best of All

A hardy, reliable swede with purple skin and yellow flesh.

Ruby

Sweet, yellow-fleshed roots with purple skin. Winter-hardy, with resistance to powdery mildew.

text:
Swede.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Autumn / Winter

Swedes are hardy brassica roots: slower, sweeter, more substantial and much more frost-resistant than turnips. Orange or yellow flesh and leaves rising from a neck help distinguish them. Cold improves their flavour for boiling, mashing and seasoning. Allow about a month longer than turnips, with room for roots to swell. June sowings can follow early lettuce, carrots, broad beans or other early crops.

Quick facts
Harvest

Sep – Apr

Germination

6–10 days

Sowing depth

Outdoor drills: about 3/4 in.

Row spacing

15 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

30 lb

Ready in

About 20–24 weeks from sowing

Sow

Jun for maincrop. May is possible. By early Jul use a variety that can still mature locally.

Plant spacing

Between plants: Maincrop: 8-10 in.; baby roots: 3-4 in.

Plant out

Jun–Jul for module-raised seedlings.

Recommended varieties
Magres

A purple-topped swede with yellow flesh and good eating quality. A strong addition for an autumn and winter root crop.

Marian

A familiar purple-topped swede with pale yellow flesh.

Tweed F1

A vigorous British-bred hybrid with clubroot resistance. Useful where that disease is a concern, alongside good rotation and soil care.

Joan

Good-flavoured roots for autumn cropping. Sow in late spring or early summer.

Best of All

A hardy, reliable swede with purple skin and yellow flesh.

Ruby

Sweet, yellow-fleshed roots with purple skin. Winter-hardy, with resistance to powdery mildew.

Key risks
Flea beetle

Young swede seedlings may be peppered with small holes.

Checked growth / poor root quality

Turnips, swedes and radishes need steady, quick growth.

Cabbage root fly

Maggots may tunnel roots.

Quality problems

Dryness, crowding, hot weather or delayed harvesting can make roots smaller, harder or fibrous.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
88
ROOT CROPS

Keep roots growing steadily.

Moist soil and early thinning give tender roots.

Prepare the bed ahead.

Use settled fertile ground; avoid fresh manure at sowing.

Soil & preparation
Choose a sunny, fertile, well-drained site. Swedes do best in cool, moist conditions; heat and drought make roots fibrous.
Add compost or well-rotted manure ahead of sowing. Prepare a fine, firm seedbed.
Sowing & planting
Sow shallow drills
Thin while small
Sow 

Make shallow drills in the final bed and sow thinly. Cover with fine soil and keep the seedbed moist. Fill a bed cleared of early salads or beans while there is still time for roots to swell.

Plant out 

Modules are an alternative if the bed is occupied. Move small seedlings before their roots fill the cells. Firm the soil and water in.

Looking after the crop
Thin early and weed carefully without damaging roots. Keep soil evenly moist; a wet spell after drought can split roots.
Mulch between established rows on light soils. Keep the soil firm but avoid a hard surface crust.
Mesh seedlings and net against birds. Check caterpillars and root-fly damage.
Harvesting & storage
Lift usable roots from September; frost improves flavour. Sound roots can stand through winter and, in mild areas, into April. Inspect them and finish before spring regrowth.
For storage, lift sound roots, twist off leaves and pack in dry sand or sacks in a cool, rodent-proof shed. Avoid repeated freezing and thawing.
Use turnips first and leave hardier swedes for later. Finish remaining roots before spring regrowth or flowering lowers quality.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Flea beetle	Tiny holes in young leaves.	Mesh seedlings; water to keep growth steady.
Cabbage root fly	Maggots tunnel roots.	Cover after sowing; discard badly damaged roots.
Quality problems	Small, hard, fibrous or split roots.	Thin early, water evenly and harvest before regrowth.
Boron deficiency	Grey-brown or hollow cores.	Confirm with a soil test; seek organic advice, never overdose.
Birds and caterpillars	Leaves stripped or chewed.	Net securely; pick off eggs and caterpillars.
Soft rot	Wet, slimy crowns; foliage collapses.	Remove affected roots; store only sound, undamaged roots.
Black rot	Yellow leaves; black veins or root rings.	Remove diseased plants; rotate and improve drainage.
Final tips

Give maincrop roots more room than baby swedes.

Store only sound roots and check them regularly.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 144–146 · Growing Techniques 150–151
